  The Model Project Constructor pipeline begins with an automated intake
  interview: an agent interviews a business stakeholder and must decide, within
  a fixed question budget, that it has learned enough to write a structured
  report. *Interview convergence* is the quality property that says that
  decision happens reliably. This document explains the live test that measures
  it --- how a single interview sample runs as a loop between two language
  models, the precise definition of "converged", the statistics layer that

# The capability and why it matters {#sec-capability}

The Model Project Constructor is a six-step pipeline that takes a business idea
from an intake interview through data collection and validation to an initial
model website, delivered as a project for a data science team. **Step 1 is the
Business Intake Interview.** An agent --- acting as an expert data scientist,
business analyst, and consultant for a **property and casualty (P&C)** insurer's
claims organization --- conducts a guided discussion with a business
stakeholder. It asks **one question at a time, up to a hard cap of 20
questions**, and converges on four output sections: the business problem, the
proposed solution, the model solution (target plus inputs), and the estimated
value.

Everything downstream depends on this step terminating *usefully*. If the
interviewer cannot decide it has enough information within the 20-question
budget, it cannot produce the structured Intake Report that Steps 2 onward
consume. **Interview convergence** is exactly that property: the interviewer
judged it had learned enough *before* exhausting the budget.

## The capability inside the evaluation gate

Convergence is one capability in a larger provider-quality gate defined in
**Section 3.4 of the multi-provider large-language-model (LLM) plan**
(hereafter **§3.4**). That gate exists to compare LLM providers --- an
`anthropic` incumbent baseline against a `bedrock` candidate --- on the same
golden corpus, so a provider cutover can be made on evidence rather than
intuition. (`bedrock` is currently skipped because no Amazon Web Services
credentials are available; the battery runs the `anthropic` half.)

The interview-convergence capability has two thresholds, single-sourced in
`eval_thresholds.py`:

```python
# tests/eval/eval_thresholds.py:30-31
INTERVIEW_CONVERGENCE_MIN = 0.95   # at least 95% of interviews converge
INTERVIEW_PREMATURE_MAX = 0        # zero early-convergence cases
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Status (as of this writing)
Convergence is **live-confirmed GREEN at 100% (20 of 20 samples)**, measured
twice through independent entry points in Session 170, and the gate is **robust
to network transport blips** after Session 171. The thresholds above were
deliberately *never lowered* to manufacture a pass --- the work described in
@sec-stats was a harness-statistics fix, not a threshold loosening.
:::


# How one interview sample runs: the two-LLM loop {#sec-loop}

A single sample means: drive a real interviewer all the way to a terminal
report, then ask whether that report shows convergence. Driving it requires a
*second* language model to play the stakeholder, because a live interviewer
generates its own questions and we cannot know them in advance.

## The two participants

1. **The interviewer** --- the intake agent under test (`IntakeAgent`). It
   generates each question itself and, at some point, records an internal
   judgment (`believe_enough_info`) that it has learned enough.
2. **The stakeholder simulator** --- `StakeholderSimulator`
   (`tests/eval/stakeholder_sim.py`), an `AnswerProvider`. Handed *whatever
   question the interviewer actually asked*, it answers from the fixture's full
   knowledge brief.

The simulator is deliberately wired to the **same provider, credentials, and
model tier** as the interviewer under test --- it reuses the interviewer's own
software development kit (SDK) client handle and resolved model identifier --- so
the two LLMs are matched:

```python
# tests/eval/stakeholder_sim.py:153-175  (stakeholder_simulator_for)
intake_client = cast(Any, make_intake_client(provider, model=model))
return StakeholderSimulator(
    brief=_brief_from_fixture(fixture),
    client=intake_client._client,   # borrow the same SDK handle ...
    model=intake_client._model,     # ... and the same resolved model id
    max_tokens=max_tokens,
)
```

The brief it answers from is assembled from everything the stakeholder could
plausibly know: the initial problem they raised, the facts established in prior
discussion (`qa_pairs`), and the **complete blessed draft** --- which carries
the value-measurement plan the interviewer must probe to converge
(`stakeholder_sim.py:69-97`). Because the simulator answers *on demand*, it can
never "run out" of answers.

## The driver loop

The live test builds one sample as a `run_one` callable:

```python
# tests/eval/test_eval_live.py:140-150  (inside test_live_interview_converges)
def run_one(case: InterviewCase) -> IntakeReport:
    fixture = load_fixture(case.fixture_path)
    agent = IntakeAgent(llm=make_intake_client(provider))
    return agent.run_scripted(
        stakeholder_id=fixture["stakeholder_id"],
        session_id=f"live-{fixture['session_id']}",
        domain=fixture.get("domain", "pc_claims"),
        initial_problem=fixture.get("initial_problem"),
        answer_provider=stakeholder_simulator_for(fixture, provider=provider),
        review_responses=review_sequence_from_fixture(fixture),
    )
```

`run_scripted` (`agent.py:68`) drives the compiled interview graph (a LangGraph
state machine) headlessly. It starts the graph, then services each *interrupt*
the graph raises until the graph's `finalize` step completes:

```
  graph.invoke(initial_state)
  repeat (bounded by max_turns = MAX_QUESTIONS + MAX_REVISIONS + 5 = 28):
      snapshot = graph.get_state()
      if no pending interrupt:  break
      if interrupt is a "question":
          reply = answer_provider(question, question_number)  # the simulator
      elif interrupt is a "review":
          reply = next(review_responses)                      # a fixed list
      graph.invoke(resume = reply)
  return build_intake_report(final_state)
```

Two answer sources are possible, and exactly one must be supplied
(`agent.py:81-98`): a fixed `interview_answers` list (used by the deterministic
tier), or an `answer_provider` (used by the live tier). The `max_turns` bound is
the only thing standing between a buggy graph and an infinite loop
(`agent.py:108-160`).

## Why the simulator exists {#sec-simulator-why}

The original deterministic approach replayed a *fixed recorded list* of answers,
one per recorded question. That only works when the questions are fixed. A live
interviewer asks more or different questions than any recorded script supplies,
so the list ran out --- `run_scripted` then raised `RuntimeError("Fixture ran
out of interview answers ...")` and the interview was scored as a
non-convergence. That was a **harness artifact**, not model behavior (recorded
in `PROJECT_LEARNINGS` #21 and the §3.4 agreement report).

The simulator (Session 166) closed that hole. Because it answers any question
on demand from the fixture's full knowledge, the script can no longer starve,
so **a sub-convergence now reflects the interviewer model's own behavior**
(`stakeholder_sim.py:1-23`).


# The convergence definition: the `questions_cap_reached` marker {#sec-definition}

Convergence is decided by a single, deliberately narrow predicate:

```python
# tests/eval/eval_scoring.py:92-107  (interview_converged)
def interview_converged(report: IntakeReport) -> bool:
    return "questions_cap_reached" not in report.missing_fields
```

So convergence is defined by the **absence** of one marker string in the
report's `missing_fields`. To trust that definition you have to know exactly
when that marker is added.

## Where the marker comes from

The interview graph's `finalize` step appends it under one precise condition:

```python
# src/model_project_constructor/agents/intake/nodes.py:131-136  (finalize_node)
if (
    asked >= MAX_QUESTIONS                       # MAX_QUESTIONS == 20
    and not state.get("believe_enough_info", False)
    and "questions_cap_reached" not in missing
):
    missing.append("questions_cap_reached")
```

Reading the condition: the marker is present **if and only if** the interview
hit the 20-question cap *without* the interviewer ever recording
`believe_enough_info`. Therefore its **absence** is precisely "the interviewer
believed it had enough information within the cap" --- which is exactly the
§3.4 metric text. (`believe_enough_info` is the interviewer LLM's own judgment,
recorded into graph state during the drafting decision, `nodes.py:58, 82`.)

## Why not gate on `status == "COMPLETE"`? (gap #1b) {#sec-gap1b}

It is tempting to call an interview "converged" when its report is `COMPLETE`.
That is wrong, and fixing it was **gap #1b** (Session 168). A report is
`COMPLETE` only when the human review was accepted *and* there are zero missing
fields (`nodes.py:154`) --- that is report **finalization**, a stricter and
*different* property than interview convergence. Gating on `COMPLETE` measured
report completeness, not whether the interview converged; the scorer was
stricter than its own §3.4 metric. Keying on the marker fixed the mismatch
(`eval_scoring.py:99-105`).

## The premature-convergence guard

The §3.4 metric also requires "zero premature convergence". A companion scorer
flags an interview that converged *too early*:

```python
# tests/eval/eval_scoring.py:110-126  (premature_convergence)
return (
    "questions_cap_reached" not in report.missing_fields  # same convergence signal
    and report.questions_asked < min_questions            # default = 2
)
```

Critically, this guard keys on the **same** convergence signal as
`interview_converged`, not on `status == "COMPLETE"`. If it keyed on `COMPLETE`,
an interview could converge at question 1 yet never finalize and so slip past
the premature check (`eval_scoring.py:117-121`).


# The statistics layer and the gap&nbsp;#1c robustness rationale {#sec-stats}

## Why "four cases, run once" was fragile (gap #1c) {#sec-fragility}

Originally, both call sites ran each interview fixture **exactly once** and
computed a pass rate over the resulting booleans against the 95% bar. There are
four converging fixtures (@sec-corpus), so the rate was a fraction over four
samples. **95% over four samples mathematically requires 4 out of 4**, because
3 out of 4 is only 75%, which is below 95%.

That made the gate brutally fragile. A *single* miss --- whether the model
genuinely wobbled once, or a one-off transient blip occurred (a truncated
application programming interface (API) response, an empty simulated answer, a
network timeout) --- dropped the gate to 75% and **failed the entire roughly
90-minute live run**. The gate was measuring luck, not capability
(`interview_sweep.py:11-15`).

## Two robustness fixes (the threshold left untouched)

`interview_sweep.py` owns the statistics of the measurement so the assertion
gate and the report producer stay in lock-step on one definition. It applies two
fixes, and explicitly **does not move the 95% bar** --- this is a
harness-statistics fix, not a threshold loosening.

**Fix 1 --- sample each case at least five times and pool the results.**

```python
# tests/eval/interview_sweep.py:64
N_SAMPLES = 5
```

This matches the discipline the governance live test already used. With five
samples per case across four cases, the pool is 20 samples, so one transient
miss is 1 in 20 (95%), not 1 in 4 (75%) --- it no longer sinks the gate
(`interview_sweep.py:111-149`).

**Fix 2 --- tell a transient blip apart from a genuine non-convergence.** A
once-off failure that is an artifact of *the call* --- not the interviewer
declining to converge --- is retried a bounded number of times and, if it still
fails, **excluded** from the sample with a logged note rather than scored as a
non-convergence:

```python
# tests/eval/interview_sweep.py:68
_MAX_TRANSIENT_RETRIES = 2   # so up to 3 attempts per sample before exclusion
```

The classification logic lives in `_run_one_sample` (`interview_sweep.py:152-180`):
it retries on a transient error, and returns `None` (the sample is excluded)
only when every attempt hit a transient error. A non-transient error is *not*
caught --- it propagates.

## The three-way outcome taxonomy

The heart of the robustness layer is a deliberate three-way split. Every sample
ends in exactly one of these outcomes:

| Outcome | What it is | Examples | Handling |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Transient** | An artifact of the API / seam / transport, not interview behavior | `IntakeLLMError` (intake client got a truncated/empty/malformed response); `StakeholderSimError` (simulator returned empty content); `APITimeoutError` / `APIConnectionError` (Anthropic SDK network blip, raised only *after* the SDK exhausts its own retries) | Retried up to 2 times; if still failing, the sample is **excluded** (counted separately, with a logged note) and never scored as a miss. |
| **Genuine non-convergence** | The interviewer returned a report carrying `questions_cap_reached` | The graph self-terminates at the 20-question cap *with a report* --- it does **not** raise | Scored `False` --- it counts against the rate, as it should. |
| **Real bug** | An API / harness / graph defect, not a model miss | `APIStatusError` (4xx/5xx: bad model id, auth, rate limit) --- a *sibling* of `APIConnectionError`, deliberately **not** caught; a non-seam `RuntimeError` (unknown interrupt, starved review script, the max-turns backstop) | **Propagates** and aborts the run. Silently scoring these `False` is what once hid harness defects as model misses. |

: Every interview sample ends in exactly one of three outcomes. {#tbl-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[14,22,36,28]"}

The transient set is single-sourced:

```python
# tests/eval/interview_sweep.py:82-87
_TRANSIENT_ERRORS: tuple[type[Exception], ...] = (
    IntakeLLMError,        # application/seam: subclass of RuntimeError
    StakeholderSimError,   # application/seam: subclass of RuntimeError
    APITimeoutError,       # transport: subclass of APIConnectionError
    APIConnectionError,    # transport
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The transport half was a residual (gap #1c, Session 171)
A transient classifier is only complete if it covers **both** application/seam
errors **and** transport errors. The original tuple held only the first two; a
live gate run then aborted on a raw `APITimeoutError` (a Secure Sockets Layer
handshake timeout) that propagated past it. Session 171 added the two transport
classes. The boundary is intentional: `APIStatusError` (a genuine 4xx/5xx API
error) is a *sibling* of `APIConnectionError`, **not** a subclass, so it is not
caught and still surfaces loudly --- guarding against the failure mode (project
"FM #18") of a catch silently swallowing real bugs
(`interview_sweep.py:70-87`).
:::

## The result, and why it is unit-testable without an API key

The sweep returns a small result object (`interview_sweep.py:96-109`):

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class InterviewSweepResult:
    convergence_results: list[bool]   # pooled per-sample pass/fail
    premature_count: int              # §3.4 premature-convergence count
    excluded_transient: int           # samples dropped after retries
```

The sweep itself **calls no LLM**. It receives a `run_one` callable that performs
one live interview, so the sampling and classification logic is deterministically
unit-tested with a fake runner (`test_interview_sweep.py`) --- no API key, no
network --- mirroring how `eval_scoring.py` keeps scoring testable
(`interview_sweep.py:42-46`). The Session 171 transport-error addition was
verified this way: four deterministic tests built from genuine SDK exception
objects, with no live run.


# The corpus, including the negative control {#sec-corpus}

The interview goldens are declared in `eval_corpus.py` and loaded by
`load_interview_cases()`:

```python
# tests/eval/eval_corpus.py:103-109  (_INTERVIEW_SOURCES)
_INTERVIEW_SOURCES = [
    ("subrogation",          .../subrogation.yaml,          True),
    ("pricing_optimization", .../pricing_optimization.yaml, True),
    ("fraud_triage",         .../fraud_triage.yaml,         True),
    ("reserving_adequacy",   .../reserving_adequacy.yaml,   True),
    ("question_cap",         .../intake_question_cap.yaml,   False),  # <- control
]
```

| `case_id` | `expect_complete` | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `subrogation` | `True` | converging --- reused project fixture |
| `pricing_optimization` | `True` | converging --- reused project fixture |
| `fraud_triage` | `True` | converging --- reused project fixture |
| `reserving_adequacy` | `True` | converging --- authored for the eval |
| `question_cap` | `False` | **negative control** (terminates at the cap) |

: The five interview goldens; the fixture paths are listed in the code block above. {#tbl-corpus tbl-colwidths="[32,20,48]"}

Three of the four converging cases reuse the project's own blessed intake
fixtures, which keeps the goldens single-sourced rather than duplicated
(`eval_corpus.py:1-17`).

## The negative-control cap fixture {#sec-negative-control}

`intake_question_cap.yaml` (`expect_complete = False`) is the inverse of a
converging case. It is engineered so the interviewer *should* spend the full
20-question budget **without** ever believing it has enough --- that is, it
should **produce** the `questions_cap_reached` marker rather than avoid it.

The live convergence sweep deliberately **skips** it, so it never dilutes the
95% rate:

```python
# tests/eval/interview_sweep.py:132-134  (sweep_interview_convergence)
for case in cases:
    if not case.expect_complete:
        continue          # the question-cap golden is not expected to converge
```

Its cap behavior is instead pinned by the **deterministic** tier, which asserts
the full inverse property:

```python
# tests/eval/test_eval_corpus.py:117-123  (test_interview_question_cap_terminates)
assert not interview_converged(report)
assert report.status == "DRAFT_INCOMPLETE"
assert "questions_cap_reached" in report.missing_fields
assert report.questions_asked == MAX_QUESTIONS    # == 20
```

(The same cap behavior is also covered at the graph level in `test_graph.py`.)

**Why a negative control matters.** A convergence metric that only ever sees
cases that *should* converge cannot distinguish "the agent converges correctly"
from "the agent always says yes." The cap fixture proves the marker actually
fires when it should --- that the convergence definition has teeth. This is the
classic negative-control discipline applied to an LLM evaluation.

## One corpus, two tiers

The same corpus feeds two test tiers. The **deterministic** tier
(`test_eval_corpus.py`) replays the fixtures with a `FixtureLLMClient` (no API
key) to prove the scorers and corpus are well-formed. The **live** tier
(@sec-callsites) runs a real provider plus the simulator. Same goldens,
different source of model behavior.


# Gate versus producer: the two call sites {#sec-callsites}

Both consumers of the corpus call the *same* helper,
`interview_sweep.sweep_interview_convergence`, so they can never drift on the
definition of convergence. They differ only in stance.

## The gate (asserts)

`test_live_interview_converges` is the assertion gate
(`test_eval_live.py:134-157`):

```python
sweep = sweep_interview_convergence(load_interview_cases(), run_one)
rate = pass_rate("interview", sweep.convergence_results)
assert rate.meets(thresholds.INTERVIEW_CONVERGENCE_MIN), (
    f"interview convergence {rate.rate:.1%} < "
    f"{thresholds.INTERVIEW_CONVERGENCE_MIN:.0%} "
    f"(n={rate.total}, excluded_transient={sweep.excluded_transient})"
)
```

It runs under `pytest -m live`, is parametrized over every shadow provider
(currently three), and is auto-skipped per provider when that provider's
credentials are absent (so continuous integration (CI), which has no
credentials, stays hermetic). A
sub-threshold result **fails the run**. The failure message reports both the
sample count and how many samples were excluded as transient.

## The producer (measures and reports)

`shadow_run.measure_provider` is the report producer
(`shadow_run.py:73-153`). It measures *every* §3.4 capability --- including the
quality-check (QC) structural metric and the Structured Query Language (SQL)
metrics --- and prints the per-capability rates plus a rendered agreement
report. It calls the same sweep:

```python
# tests/eval/shadow_run.py:139-141
sweep = sweep_interview_convergence(
    load_interview_cases(), _run_interview, n_samples=n_samples, on_event=_warn
)
```

Crucially, the producer **does not assert**. A sub-threshold number is recorded
as *data* (a no-go signal), not a failed run, so it can fill the cutover report
and compare providers side by side. The committed go/no-go lives in
`PHASE_E_AGREEMENT_REPORT.md`, fed by `eval_cutover.evaluate_cutover`
(`shadow_run.py:1-22`, `156-183`). It is run explicitly, for example:

```bash
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=… uv run python tests/eval/shadow_run.py
# (run from the repo root, or set PYTHONPATH=.)
```

## Why have both

An assertion gate is binary --- ideal for CI, useless for filling a report. A
producer yields the actual numbers and must *not* "fail" merely because a
candidate is sub-threshold (that is data, not an error). Same definition, two
stances.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The two-draw insight (Session 170)
Because both entry points share the sampling helper, one `shadow_run` *is* the
gate's convergence verdict. But running **two independent draws through
different entry points** is not redundant --- it tests robustness *across* runs,
which is the very concern of a fragility fix. It was the second draw (the gate)
that surfaced the uncaught transport-timeout residual closed in @sec-stats. A
subject-matter expert (SME) reviewing such a gate should expect the second draw
to earn its keep.
:::
